Lecture 13 The Exponential Distribution, Its Link to the Poisson Distribution, and Jointly Distributed Random Variables

The exponential distribution from its pdf through the mean, the variance, the cdf and the memoryless property, then the fact that Poisson counts and exponential waiting times are two views of the same process; after the break, the first look at two random variables measured on one experiment: the joint table, the marginal distributions and a conditional distribution.

We can model the length of time until a light bulb fails using an exponential random variable.

If the light bulb is left on and measures the time until it fails, then

6Jointly distributed random variables

Jointly Distributed Random Variables

Sometimes we assign more than one value to the outcome of an experiment, or to a sample member that is “selected”.

Example

Suppose we draw a simple random sample of 2 cards from a standard deck of 52 playing cards and sample without replacement.

Let be the random variable that counts the number of hearts and be the random variable that counts the number of aces.

Explanation (added) ✎

One experiment, two numbers. The pair of cards drawn gives both (0, 1 or 2 aces) and (0, 1 or 2 hearts). The two are linked because the ace of hearts counts toward both. A joint distribution describes the pair instead of each variable separately.

Textbook Devore §5.1, p. 199: “more than one random variable (rv) will be of interest to an investigator”; the first case studied is two discrete rv’s.

The board says “joint pdf” and writes , then . For discrete variables Devore calls it the joint pmf, , p. 199.
Explanation (added) ✎

Every cell is a count out of equally likely pairs of cards. Exact counts: (rows , columns ). For example:

: two aces with exactly one heart means the ace of hearts plus one of the other 3 aces, so 3 pairs.
: one ace and two hearts means the ace of hearts plus one of the other 12 hearts, so 12 pairs.
: both cards are neither an ace nor a heart (36 such cards).
: two aces cannot both be hearts.

All nine counts add to 1326, so the exact probabilities add to 1; the board’s rounded entries add to 0.999 (see the marginals).

  • An exponential model with a given rate or mean: find , or with , and state the mean and standard deviation.
  • Derive and for the exponential pdf by integration by parts (your note says the instructor plans this).
  • State the memoryless property, prove it in two lines, or explain it for a light bulb or a waiting time.

Six questions on this lecture, written for this page with new numbers, in the style of the “typical exam question” list above. Work each one on paper first, then open the answer. Tick the ones you got; the tally is remembered on this device.

0 of 6 ticked
  1. Exam-styleReview: section 1 · Exponential

    The time X (minutes) until the next customer arrives is exponential with λ = 0.5.

    Find P(X ≤ 1), P(X > 3), P(1 < X < 3), and the mean and standard deviation.

    Show the worked answer

    F(x) = 1 − e−λx, and the tail is P(X > c) = e−λc.

    P(X ≤ 1) = 1 − e−0.5 ≈ 0.3935.

    P(X > 3) = e−1.5 ≈ 0.2231.

    P(1 < X < 3) = e−0.5 − e−1.5 ≈ 0.6065 − 0.2231 = 0.3834.

    Mean = 1/λ = 2 minutes, and the standard deviation is also 1/λ = 2 minutes.

    Check: the three probabilities add to 1.

  2. JustifyReview: section 2 · Memoryless

    State the memoryless property and prove it. Then: a bulb’s lifetime is exponential with mean 1000 hours and it has already lasted 500 hours. What is the probability it lasts at least 1000 more?

    Show the worked answer

    Property: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).

    Proof: if X > s + t then certainly X > s, so the intersection is just {X > s + t}. By the conditional probability formula,

    P(X > s + t)P(X > s) = e−λ(s + t)e−λs = e−λt = P(X > t).

    Bulb: λ = 1/1000. The 500 hours already survived do not matter: P = e−1000/1000 = e−1 ≈ 0.368, the same as for a new bulb.

  3. Exam-styleReview: section 3 · Mean free path

    a) For any exponential random variable, find the probability that it is less than half its mean.
    b) Five independent exponential distances are measured. What is the probability that exactly 2 of them are less than half the mean?

    Show the worked answer

    a) The mean is 1/λ, so half the mean is 1/(2λ). P(X < 1/(2λ)) = 1 − e−λ · 1/(2λ) = 1 − e−1/2 ≈ 0.3935. The λ cancels, so this is true for every λ.

    b) Each distance is “short” with probability 0.3935, independently, so the count Y ~ Bin(5, 0.3935).

    P(Y = 2) = (5 choose 2)(0.3935)²(0.6065)³ ≈ 0.3454. TI-84: binompdf(5, 0.3935, 2).

  4. Exam-styleReview: section 4 · Exponential & Poisson

    Customers arrive at a counter following a Poisson process at 30 per hour.

    a) What is the distribution of the wait (in minutes) between customers, and its mean?
    b) Find the probability of waiting more than 5 minutes, two ways.

    Show the worked answer

    a) 30 per hour is λ = 0.5 per minute. The wait X is exponential(0.5), with mean 1/λ = 2 minutes.

    b) Exponential: P(X > 5) = e−0.5 × 5 = e−2.5 ≈ 0.0821.

    Poisson: waiting more than 5 minutes means no arrivals in 5 minutes. The count in 5 minutes is Poisson with μ = 0.5 × 5 = 2.5, and P(count = 0) = e−2.5. Same number, which is the link between the two distributions.

  6. JustifyReview: section 1 · Exponential

    Your note says the instructor plans this one. Use integration by parts to show that an exponential random variable has E(X) = 1/λ.

    Show the worked answer

    E(X) = ∫0∞ x λe−λx dx. Take u = x and dv = λe−λx dx, so du = dx and v = −e−λx.

    E(X) = [−x e−λx] from 0 to ∞ + ∫0∞ e−λx dx.

    The bracket is 0 at both ends (at ∞ the exponential beats x; at 0 the factor x is 0).

    The remaining integral is [−e−λx/λ] from 0 to ∞ = 1/λ. So E(X) = 1/λ.

    The variance needs parts twice for E(X²) = 2/λ², giving 2/λ² − 1/λ² = 1/λ²; the page’s reveal in Section 1 has it.
